summary:
IRIS (Infrared Remote Incident System) is a Progressive Web App (PWA) that displays current and historical wildfires on an interactive globe. Its purpose is to alert the public to active fires and to give scientists and the general community easy access to reliable fire data.

The platform combines near-real-time satellite detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS) with a harmonized MODIS + VIIRS archive dating back to November 2000. This lets users follow fires as they happen and compare them against more than two decades of history. Users can filter by country, area, date, time, severity and heat source (vegetation, industrial sites, volcanoes or offshore oil), and browse a year–month–day timeline. A live mode alerts them to new hotspots, and a risk-estimation panel lets them test how weather and vegetation conditions affect fire risk. Results can be exported as CSV for further analysis. The app is bilingual (English and Spanish) and installable on any device as a PWA.
details:
What it does and how it works

IRIS (Infrared Remote Incident System) is a Progressive Web App that shows current and historical wildfires and other thermal anomalies on an interactive 3D globe. A Node.js/Express backend reads a harmonized MODIS + VIIRS archive, stored in Google Cloud Storage as monthly country files dating back to November 2000. It merges that archive with near-real-time NASA FIRMS detections (VIIRS NOAA-20) and serves the result to the app. Users can filter by country, drawn or searched area, radius, date, time of day, severity and heat source. They can also browse a year–month–day timeline with animated playback and jump to the peak day. A live mode refreshes every minute and alerts users to new hotspots. Each hotspot is classified by Fire Radiative Power into five levels, from Low to Extreme. An experimental risk panel lets users adjust temperature, humidity, wind, days without rain and dry vegetation to see how conditions change an estimated risk score. Results can be exported as CSV or as a regional HTML report.

Benefits and intended impact

The public gets a clear, visual way to see where fires are burning now. Scientists and the wider community get free, filterable access to more than two decades of data, without handling raw satellite files. We hope it makes fire information easier to find and understand, supports awareness and early attention to active fires, and helps people compare today’s activity against the historical record for the same place and month.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Angular, Ionic, TypeScript, Mapbox GL JS, RxJS, Angular Service Worker.
  • Backend: Node.js, Express, Google Cloud Storage SDK, axios, csv-parser, country-coder.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS API and MODIS/VIIRS active fire data.
  • Deployment: Render.
  • No special hardware was used; all detections come from satellite data.

Creativity

Beyond plotting fire points, IRIS separates likely heat sources: vegetation, recurring industrial sites, active volcanoes and offshore oil areas. This reduces confusion between wildfires and other persistent heat. It also compares each fire’s intensity against the history of its country and month, and offers a globe view with live alerts and optional ambient music.

Factors we considered

  • Performance at scale: a streaming backend, parallel reads and multi-level caching (memory, disk and cloud) keep queries fast over millions of records.
  • Accessibility: it is a PWA that installs on any device and is bilingual (English and Spanish).
  • Data quality: unified schema, duplicate removal and intensity thresholds.
  • Responsible communication: the risk panel is exploratory and not an official forecast.
